newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts welcome Incentive's sharper focus.
newsitem.headline: Analysts welcome Incentive's sharper focus.

text.p: Swedish company Incentive's sale of half its stake in ABB AB was in line with the company's policy to unravel non-core investments and focus on medical technology, analysts said on Thursday.

Incentive announced late Wednesday that it was selling the stake for 12.4 billion crowns ($1.6 billion) to institutions and investment group Investor, a fellow runner in the stable of Sweden's powerful Wallenberg family.
"It is just a case of refocusing on medical technology as they have promised," analyst Peter Bradshaw of Merrill Lynch told Reuters.
"It is nothing more than that. There is no hidden agenda."
A Stockholm based analyst said Incentive wanted to get rid of all its investments and concentrate on medical technology.
"In the longterm it will be just involved in the medical technology area but this will take a long time," she said.
Merrill Lynch recommends investors accumulate stock in Incentive which has just become one of the world's largest kidney-case groups through acquiring U.S. Vivra Inc.
"We still think Incentive is good value around these levels," Bradshaw said. "The market has been very efficient today at pricing in the gains from this deal."
Incentive share rose 21 crowns on Thursday to 728 crowns.
The company sold 6.5 billion crowns worth of ABB shares to Investor at the June 11 closing price of 114.5 crowns which keeps control of ABB AB in the Wallenberg sphere.

The other six billion crowns worth were sold to Morgan Stanley Dean Witter to sell to institutions. The investment bank said on Thursday it would sell the shares at 111 crowns, a three percent discount on June 11's closing price.

Another analyst, who asked not to be named, said the sale was not a surprise but came earlier than expected. Incentive was expected to sell off the rest of its ABB shares after February 1998 and Investor has already expressed interest to acquire more.
"It depends on how they find a solution not to pay too much on capital gains tax," the analyst said.
Since wholly acquiring international dialysis and medical technology group Gambro in March 1996, Incentive has embarked on a programme to divest non-strategic holdings.

In 1996 it sold off stakes in camera company Hasselblad, automotive components group Garphyttan, trading company AKA, and electricity company Skandinaviska Elverk (SEV) -- equivalent to about 30 percent of the group.
This year it has sold subsidiary TA Hydronics and its holding in U.S. company Westinghouse Air Brake Company.
Analysts expected Incentive to divest its holding in Swedish appliance maker Electrolux and sell its Hagglunds Vehicle operation as already mooted by the company.
Incentive said the 9.9 billion crown capital gain from the sale of ABB shares would replace the money spent by the company on acquiring U.S. dialysis unit Vivra.
This week Incentive announced it had completed its cash tender offer to buy Vivra which it plans to merge into the Gambro Group.
The combination of Vivra and Gambro unit Gambro Healthcare wil create a leading renal care company with 380 clinics in the U.S. treating about 26,000 patients.
-- Belinda Goldsmith, Stockholm newsrom +46-8-700 1045 ($ = 7.774 Swedish Crowns)
